name: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
what: This subtopic covers Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) as a biological model of stress with three stages: alarm reaction (shock and counter shock), resistance, and exhaustion. It also addresses the explanatory power of the model, including its strengths and limitations.
why: The GAS is the key biological model of stress in the VCE study design. Understanding the distinct physiological characteristics of each stage, including the role of cortisol, allows students to apply the model to scenarios and evaluate it critically.

items.title: I can describe the overall structure of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
items.what: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) is a biological model involving three stages of physiological reactions in response to a persistent stressor: alarm reaction, resistance, and exhaustion. The alarm reaction stage has two substages: shock and counter shock.
items.why: Knowing the structure before the detail of each stage is required because exam questions often ask students to name stages in order, identify which stage a person is in, or write out the full name and acronym correctly on first use.
items.example: In an exam answer: 'Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) proposes that when Bob first encountered the stressor he entered the alarm reaction stage...'

items.title: I can describe the shock and counter shock substages of the alarm reaction
items.what: Shock is the first substage in which bodily arousal briefly drops below normal following initial exposure to a stressor: body temperature, blood pressure, and muscle tone temporarily decrease. Counter shock follows immediately, with sympathetic nervous system activation causing adrenaline and cortisol release, raising arousal above normal.
items.why: Exam questions often present a scenario and ask students to identify both the stage and the substage. Identifying alarm reaction without specifying the substage is insufficient for full marks.
items.example: Sophie crashes her car. Immediately after impact she freezes and cannot think clearly (shock). Seconds later her heart pounds, she feels a rush of adrenaline, and she is able to exit the vehicle and exchange details (counter shock).

items.title: I can describe the resistance stage of the GAS
items.what: In the resistance stage, bodily arousal remains above normal as the body adjusts to and maintains a heightened physiological state. Elevated cortisol sustains this arousal. The body directs most of its resources toward the initial stressor, reducing resistance to additional stressors. Mild illness may develop due to beginning immune suppression.
items.why: Resistance is commonly confused with exhaustion in exam responses. The key distinction is that in resistance the person can still cope with the demands of the stressor despite showing early signs of stress-related illness.
items.example: A student facing ongoing study pressure develops occasional headaches and catches a cold, but continues to attend school, study, and meet deadlines. This indicates resistance, not exhaustion.

items.title: I can describe the exhaustion stage of the GAS
items.what: In exhaustion, bodily resources including energy and stress hormones are depleted after prolonged exposure to the stressor. Arousal drops below normal, the person can no longer cope with the stressor, and immune suppression is severe. Serious physiological and psychological illness may develop, including cardiovascular disease, extreme fatigue, anxiety, and depression.
items.why: Distinguishing exhaustion from resistance requires understanding that exhaustion involves an inability to cope and serious illness, not merely mild symptoms. This distinction is directly tested using scenario-based questions.
items.example: After months of sustained financial and workplace stress, a person is diagnosed with a heart condition, is unable to go to work, and feels completely unable to manage daily demands. This indicates exhaustion.

items.title: I can explain the role of cortisol across the stages of the GAS
items.what: Cortisol is released during counter shock to energise the body. Its sustained presence during resistance maintains heightened arousal but begins suppressing immune functioning. By exhaustion, cortisol and other stress hormones are depleted, contributing to the collapse of the body's ability to respond.
items.why: Cortisol links the GAS to the physiological content from lesson 3A and appears in multiple exam questions asking students to identify its role at a specific stage.
items.example: During resistance, Winnie's sustained cortisol levels keep her functioning under exam pressure but result in recurring viral infections as her immune system is suppressed.

items.title: I can evaluate the explanatory power of Selye's GAS by identifying its strengths and limitations
items.what: Strengths: the GAS identifies a measurable, predictable pattern of physiological responses and recognises the link between chronic stress and illness. Limitations: the model was based on rat studies (reducing generalisability to humans), ignores psychological factors such as cognition and emotion, and applies a uniform model to all individuals, failing to account for individual differences in stress responses.
items.why: Evaluating the GAS is explicitly required by the study design and directly assessed in exam questions. Understanding that a biological model's strength is also its limitation relative to a psychological model is a key insight.
items.example: A strength: the GAS correctly predicts that a person under prolonged stress will develop immune suppression. A limitation: it cannot explain why two people facing the same stressor for the same duration may progress through the stages at different rates.
